idiom_name: predicate function pointer plus context (msg_filter_t), or a kernel BPF program
implementation_notes: C has neither closures nor generics, so the filter is data you write yourself: a struct holding `bool (*match)(const msg_t *, void *)` and its context, called on the branch between receive and forward - the classic filter component reduced to a function pointer. Where the message is a packet the same criterion can be pushed below the boundary: a classic or extended BPF program attached with SO_ATTACH_FILTER / SO_ATTACH_BPF via setsockopt(2) drops non-matching packets before user space sees them, and libpcap's pcap_compile/pcap_setfilter does the same for captured traffic. Both forms keep the criterion as replaceable data, which is the pattern's real benefit; hand-writing the branch stays right when the criterion is per-connection, when rejects must be counted in process, or when no BPF-capable layer exists.
pitfalls: The context pointer is the only place per-filter state can live; parking it in a global silently breaks as soon as two filters share a process or thread pool.

A filter attached with SO_ATTACH_FILTER/SO_ATTACH_BPF drops non-matching packets invisibly and a filter program that runs off the end of the buffer rejects silently - count rejects in user space when they matter.
The predicate must not read past the received length: a partially filled msg_t makes a body-based criterion read uninitialised memory.
